rules.t: One collection = one taxon, one substrate, one spot. Pick the genus, say what it was growing on and out of what, then tap the characters you actually observed.
saprotroph — litter/soil Agaricus — Free gills going pink then chocolate, a ring, and a chocolate-brown print.usual substrate soil · host grass, litter, soil · print chocolate
Substrate and host are the two characters a herbarium cannot recover later and a photograph rarely shows. For an ectomycorrhizal fungus the host is half the identification.
There is no taste field and no edibility field. That is deliberate — see Method.
Nothing recorded yet.
A fungal survey without the stand it was walked in, and without the rain that triggered it, is a list of names rather than data.
Dominant trees are not scenery. Enter them, and the host column on the Analysis tab becomes a testable association rather than an anecdote.
Most temperate macrofungi fruit on a lag after a soil-wetting rain, within a temperature window. Record the trigger, not just the day you walked.

The lag window this page reads against — a wetting event of ≥25 mm and a flush 7–21 days later — is a placeholder rule of thumb, not a calibrated model. Lags differ by guild, genus, elevation and soil. Replace the numbers with your own once you have two seasons of your own site's data; until then treat the readout as a prompt to think, not a prediction.
Choose a collection, then record the two things that cannot be got from a photograph.
A print from a young cap can read paler than the true colour, and a thin print reads paler than a thick one. Judge the colour where the deposit is heaviest, in daylight, against white.
Record what you saw and where you put it. Blank means not tested — which is not the same as negative, and the export keeps them apart.
These reagents separate species within a genus. Almost none of them separate genera, and none of them identifies anything on its own.

KOH is caustic and will damage an eye instantly. Phenol is toxic by skin absorption and by vapour. Melzer's reagent contains chloral hydrate and is controlled in some jurisdictions. Work outdoors or with ventilation, use dropper bottles rather than open dishes, wear eye protection, and do not carry reagents loose in a basket with your specimens.

A collection with a voucher number exports as PreservedSpecimen; one without exports as HumanObservation. The sheet will not call a photograph a specimen. Working names are exported as written — if the name still ends in sp. or cf., that is what a herbarium reading the file needs to see.
A fungal voucher is a race against rot. Describe it fresh, dry it fast, label it with what the dried specimen will have lost.

40–45 °C with airflow is the conventional working compromise — a convention, not a measurement, as the note below argues. It straddles the lower edge of the 43–50 °C (110–120 °F) window the Fungal Diversity Survey's collection guide recommends for specimens you may want to sequence — only its top two degrees are inside it. Below about 35 °C a fleshy cap can spoil before it is dry, which is a rule

The upper end is less settled than it is usually stated. The practitioner advice — stay under 50 °C, DNA is damaged above about 68 °C — is what most keys and forays will tell you. But Wang, Liu and Xu (Scientific Reports, 2017) dried mushrooms at seven temperatures from 22 °C to 93 °C and got successful PCR at every one of them, losing measurable double-stranded DNA only at 80–93 °C; they recommen

A fruit body is the reproductive organ of a mycelium that may be decades old and hectares wide, so picking it is closer to picking an apple than to pulling a plant — but the litter layer it sits in is not. Lift the whole fruit body, including the stipe base, because the volva, the bulb and the rhizomorphs are diagnostic and a knife-cut collection throws them away. Then put the duff back. Leave und
Every number this page produces, and what each one is worth.

Guild is assigned here at genus level, which is the level a field sheet can honestly work at. Roughly: ectomycorrhizal fungi trade soil nutrients for host carbon and fruit near a compatible tree; saprotrophs decay dead material, and it matters whether that is wood or litter, because the two respond to different weather; parasites take carbon from a living host; mycoparasites take it from another f

The strongest field evidence for ectomycorrhizal status is not the genus at all: it is a fruit body arising from soil within the rooting zone of a compatible host with no wood beneath it. That is why substrate, host and distance-to-stem are on the record form.

Observed richness Sobs is the number of distinct taxa you recorded. It is an underestimate of the fruiting community and a severe underestimate of the mycelial one: a fungus that did not fruit on the day you walked is invisible to this method, and sequencing of the same soil routinely returns several times as many species as a season of fruit-body surveys.

Chao1 estimates how many taxa the survey missed, from how many you saw exactly once and exactly twice. With F1 singletons and F2 doubletons the bias-corrected form is Chao1 = S_obs + F1·(F1−1) / (2·(F2+1)) A large gap between Sobs and Chao1 means the survey is nowhere near saturation. It does not mean the estimate is precise: Chao1 is a lower bound on true richness, it assumes your samples are ind

Shannon H′ is computed on fruit-body counts with natural logs, H′ = −Σ p_i ln p_i, and Pielou J′ = H′ / ln S. Counts of fruit bodies are a proxy for abundance with a known bias: one Armillaria genet can put up two hundred caps while a Cortinarius puts up two, so H′ on this data describes the display, not the community.

Productivity is collections and fresh mass per unit of searched area, and per unit of search time. Both are worth recording because they fail differently: area-based figures need an honestly bounded search area, and time-based figures are comparable only between searchers of similar experience and speed.

The host table cross-tabulates taxon against the host you recorded. A taxon whose collections all fall under one host is flagged, but the flag is a prompt, not a finding: with three collections under one host in a stand that is 90% that host — figures indicative, not measured — you have learned nothing about specificity, only about the stand. The comparison that means something is a taxon found re

The print is the single most informative macroscopic character on an agaric, and it is the one most often skipped because it costs hours. Colour groups here run white → cream → pink → ochre/rust → clay → brown → purple-brown → chocolate → black, plus olive-brown for the boletes and the notorious dull green of Chlorophyllum molybdites. When a print colour contradicts the genus you picked, the page

A large share of the genera in this pack cannot be taken to species in the field by anyone. Cortinarius, Inocybe, Russula, Entoloma, Mycena and most crusts need spore measurements and ornamentation, the amyloid or dextrinoid reaction in Melzer's, cystidia, pileipellis structure, and often sequencing. This sheet is built to capture the characters that disappear on drying — latex, odour, colour chan

The 65 genera loaded here cover the Pacific Northwest through the Sierra to the Great Basin. They are data, not code: export the pack from the Analysis tab to see the schema, edit it, and import it back. Import validates every field and refuses the whole file with a list of what is wrong rather than half-loading it. Copy the AI prompt produces a prompt carrying the schema and the honesty constrain
